sentences.text: One estimate suggests Amargatitanis reached around 12 meters (39.7 feet) in length and weighed 3.5 metric tons.
However, another study estimated Amargatitanis's mass at 11.406 metric tons, which is slightly larger than the estimate for Amargasaurus in the same research.
As a dicraeosaurid, Amargatitanis likely resembled Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, featuring shorter necks and long neural spines extending from the neck and trunk vertebrae.
The femur of Amargatitanis is distinctive because it is much wider at the upper end than the lower end, unlike other sauropods where the ends are approximately equal in width.
The tibia of Amargatitanis has a low cnemial crest, similar to Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, unlike the higher crest found in most macronarians.
Analysis of growth marks in a femur indicates that the Amargatitanis specimen was at least 19 years old when it died.
The unusually high number of growth marks in Amargatitanis suggests that some sauropods may have grown discontinuously rather than continuously.
Amargatitanis is a dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Barremian-aged La Amarga Formation in Neuquén, Argentina.
Argentine paleontologist José Bonaparte unearthed the remains in 1983, and they were later described as Amargatitanis macni by Sebastián Apesteguía.
The genus name Amargatitanis combines "Amarga," the location of the fossils, and "titanis," meaning "titan."
The species name macni honors the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales (MACN), where the fossils are stored.
The holotype specimen was cataloged under the number MACN PV N53 at the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales.
The skeleton remained undescribed until 2007, when it was named Amargatitanis macni by Sebastián Apesteguía.
Sebastián Apesteguía erroneously assigned a scapula and six caudal vertebrae found in 1986 to the specimen, despite them coming from different rock layers.
Amargatitanis fossils were discovered in 1983 in the La Amarga Formation by José Fernando Bonaparte.
The known fossil remains of Amargatitanis include six tail vertebrae, a femur, a scapula, and an astragalus.
The formal description of Amargatitanis was published in 2007 by the Argentine paleontologist Sebastián Apesteguía.
Evidence from neck and inner ear anatomy suggests Amargatitanis fed at heights of up to 2.7 meters.
Originally assigned to Titanosauria, a 2016 reanalysis demonstrated that Amargatitanis is a dicraeosaurid dipolodocoid.
In 2022, Guillermo Windholz and colleagues argued that Amargatitanis was especially closely related to Pilmatueia and Bajadasaurus within a South American dicraeosaurid clade.
A 2016 re-evaluation by Pablo Ariel Gallina reclassified Amargatitanis as a dicraeosaurid.
Amargatitanis is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae.
The parent group of the genus Amargatitanis is the family Dicraeosauridae.
Amargatitanis lived approximately 129 to 123 million years ago in the Barremian-aged Puesto Antigual Member of the La Amarga Formation.
Amargatitanis lived approximately 130 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Barremian stage in what is now South America.
Amargatitanis fossils come from the La Amarga Formation in the Neuquén Basin, dating to the Barremian and late Aptian of the Early Cretaceous.
Amargatitanis lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian stage.
Researchers debated whether Amargatitanis was a titanosaurian, noting that its holotype and syntypes were found in different locations and lacked valid titanosaurian characteristics.
